description: Grupo multidisciplinario, enfocado a mejorar el mundo de como lo encontramos.
summary:
PACHA es una aplicación web abierta, sin cuentas ni instalación, que explica y muestra cómo un radar de apertura sintética de banda L, como NISAR, detecta el cambio en el territorio ecuatoriano. Su lema es «La tierra guarda las marcas; el radar las lee».

La aplicación desarrolla dos historias principales: embalses y lluvia (Mazar y Daule-Peripa, con la cantidad de agua que almacenan y su variación según la lluvia y la sequía) e incendios forestales (el cerro Casitagua, junto a Quito). En torno a ellas ofrece un observatorio para comparar pasadas del satélite, un simulador de eventos y una sección didáctica para aprender a interpretar una imagen de radar.
details:
Ecuador’s territory is in constant flux: reservoirs rise and fall with the rains, forests burn, and soils become saturated. Many of these changes are difficult to observe with optical sensors, because clouds blanket much of the country for most of the year. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) systems, such as the one aboard the NISAR mission, overcome this limitation: they illuminate the surface themselves and record its structure and moisture in any weather. PACHA was created to bring this technology within reach of anyone who has never seen a radar image.

Application Walkthrough

1. Home

The landing page states the idea in a single sentence and offers one main action: to enter the reservoir story. It includes a schematic west-to-east profile of Ecuador (Pacific, Coast, Highlands, Amazon) marking the three study sites. Selecting a site opens a short note on its location and on what the radar is expected to reveal there.

An animated pass log illustrates the central concept: each layer is one satellite pass, and the most recent one is stacked on top of the earlier ones. A locator map shows the swath of roughly 240 km covered by the radar. On a first visit, a short guide opens and points out each area of the screen.

2. Stories (Explore → Stories)

This is the core of the application. Each story proceeds in four steps, each with a headline, an explanatory sentence, and a computed figure:

  • Data: a water mask for each date (shown in blue) and the reservoir surface area, obtained by summing its water pixels.
  • What the satellite sees: the HH and HV polarization signals, before and after. Calm water reflects the radar pulse away from the sensor and appears dark, so the reservoir boundary remains sharp even under cloud cover.
  • Simulate: the effect of several months of rainfall on the terrain, showing the water level rising or falling (under development, marked as “coming soon”).
  • Impacts: the shoreline change between two dates and what it may imply. For real data, findings are always framed as hypotheses to be verified with the reservoir operator, never as conclusions.

The wildfire story uses a before/after slider: cross-polarized backscatter (HV) drops where the forest loses structure. Every technical term (radar, L-band, dB, HH, HV) has a pop-up explanation in plain language.

3. Observatory (Explore → Observatory)

A general-purpose tool covering the six types of change that NISAR can detect. The user selects a change type, a scenario, and any two passes, and the application computes what changed and by how much. It offers four views: change map, before and after, time series with playback, and impact.

Users can measure a quadrant of the map and adjust model parameters (random seed, number of looks, orbit direction, and seasonality). The tool also provides site context: region, province, wet or dry season, estimated soil moisture, and monthly precipitation. Climate data come from NASA POWER and are identified as complementary information, not radar-derived. All outputs can be exported: a PNG of the comparison, a CSV of the measurements, and a PNG impact report.

4. Event Simulator

A simulated world built on real Ecuadorian terrain (SRTM), with grid cells and inhabitants, in which an event can be triggered with a click or from the keyboard: wildfire, storm, flood, earthquake, or eruption. Each phenomenon has core controls (wind and fuel moisture, rainfall, discharge, magnitude, volcanic explosivity index, among others) as well as advanced options. Users can found a city and observe how the event affects its population.

The “radar twin” shows what a radar such as NISAR would see before and after the event, comparing the detection with the simulated ground truth. An additional section addresses the question of when the radar would detect the event, depending on the revisit frequency. An event log records everything that happens. The simulator is entirely synthetic and is labeled as such.

5. Learn

  • Fundamentals: the minimum needed to read a radar image: how a radar provides its own illumination, what each type of change looks like, polarizations and bands, and the NISAR mission.
  • Laboratory: two interactive experiments. “Clouds Don’t Stop It” increases cloud cover and compares the change seen by an optical sensor with that seen by radar. “Polarization and Band” lets users switch the band (L or S) and the polarization to see how each surface responds.
  • 90-second tour: six guided steps embedding real application screens (the problem, clouds, polarization, change map, wildfire, and simulator).

Highlights

  • Data integrity. Every layer, series, and export states its origin and provenance (product, date, polarization, frequency, and maturity level). A real data layer without complete provenance is not displayed. The simulator and the laboratory are labeled “Simulation,” and anything about NISAR that has not been verified is marked “pending confirmation against official documentation.”
  • Serverless operation. On GitHub Pages, the Python API runs directly in the browser (Pyodide in a Web Worker). The scientific core stays in Python, and the site remains static and free to host.
  • Accessible and multilingual. The interface is available in Spanish, English, and Kichwa (the latter pending validation by native speakers), with keyboard navigation and a custom design system for three screen widths (desktop, tablet, and mobile).
  • Open and reproducible. Application state is stored in the URL, so any view can be shared as a link. Small derived products are versioned together with their procedencia.json provenance file, and raw HDF5 files are never committed to the repository.
  • Learning by doing. Every technical term is explained where it appears, since the intended audience is anyone who has never seen a radar image.

NISAR images of Cerro Casitagua show changes in the RFDI before (09/13/2026) and after (09/25/2026) the fire. Before the event, high values predominated (>0.4545), whereas afterward a greater presence of low values (<0.3794) is observed. These differences could be related to changes in vegetation structure, although they require validation using other indices, such as dNBR.

For the analysis of the Casitagua hill forest fire, two satellite images acquired by the NISAR synthetic aperture radar were used, dated September 13 and 25, 2026, with a 12-day interval between them. The images contain HH and HV polarization information, which was used to calculate the Radar Forest Degradation Index (RFDI). The first acquisition represents the conditions prior to the September 17 fire, while the second makes it possible to assess the subsequent changes in the radar response of the vegetation and the surface.

Data and Technology

The L-band products (GCOV, HH, and HV) come from the NISAR catalog at the ASF DAAC. The team segments water using its own method, and the application only reads those results.

The frontend is built with React 18, Vite, and TypeScript. The scientific core and API are written in Python (FastAPI) behind an interchangeable data contract. Credits for data sources, typefaces, and references are listed in CREDITOS.md.
dataRefs: NASA Earthdata Search: Earthdata Search enables data discovery, search, comparison, visualization, and access across NASA's Earth science data holdings.
ASF Data Search Vertex: The Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) operates the NASA archive of SAR data and provides services to researchers supporting NASA's ESDIS project.
NISAR Data User Guide: This guide from ASF aims to help those who research and monitor the Earth find all the information they need to know about accessing and working with NISAR data in one place.
Intro to Remote Sensing: Learn the basics about remotely-sensed data, from instrument characteristics to different types of resolution to data processing and analysis.
Intro to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR): Learn the basics about SAR data, from the roles of frequency and wavelength to polarization and scattering mechanisms.

NASA ARSET Trainings: Online trainings for beginners and advanced practitioners alike, across a breadth of topics including disaster management, ecological forecasting, agriculture, public health, air quality, and water resources management. Includes introductory materials for remote sensing, SAR, and NISAR in English and Spanish.
NISAR StoryMaps: Interactive StoryMaps on SAR applications for floods, wildfires, land subsidence, oil slicks, and glacial motion.
NISAR Applications White Papers: Brief 2-page overviews of relevant applications of NISAR data that provide societal benefit as identified by past NISAR Applications Workshops.
UAVSAR Postcards: False color composites of airborne UAVSAR data depicting various Earth processes.
projectRefs: Radarsat Constellation Mission (RCM) - Data: The RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) is Canada's new generation of Earth observation satellites. The RCM includes a trio of Earth observation satellites, capable of scanning Earth day or night and in any weather conditions. The RCM is designed to provide effective solutions in three main areas: Maritime surveillance (ice, surface wind, oil pollution and ship monitoring); Disaster management (mitigation, warning, response and recovery); and Ecosystem monitoring (agriculture, wetlands, forestry and coastal change monitoring).
Synthetic Aperture Radar python Tutorial: This tutorial demonstrates how to work with SAR imagery using Python and QGIS. It includes easy and practical steps for accessing and visualizing data.

RADARSAT 1 - Data: Launched in November 1995, RADARSAT-1 provided Canada and the world with an operational radar satellite system capable of timely delivery of large amounts of data. Equipped with a powerful synthetic aperture radar (SAR) instrument, it acquired images of the Earth day or night, in all weather and through cloud cover, smoke, and haze. All data products in the Canadian RADARSAT-1 archive have been released under an open license.

SAOCOM Catalogue: Access CONAE's latest SAR mission, SAOCOM catalogue and general information to register, download the images. Download and processing tutorials. Register for a ONE CLICK Login Profile.
SAOCOM Catalogue Registration: Registration protocol to access SAOCOM catalogue with ONE CLICK Profile.
